opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the deepest reason is that science, at bottom, is about two things: equations and reasoning. Physicists write down equations, and very often those equations are tensor equations. Think of Einstein's field equations, or Maxwell's equations, or quantum mechanics, which is basically linear algebra on very large spaces. And then on the other side, a lot of science is about rules and logical structure. Chemistry has rules about how molecules react, biology has regulatory networks, and so on. Historically we've had completely separate tools for those two things. You had numerical languages and libraries for the math, and you had logic programming or symbolic systems for the reasoning, and they didn't talk to each other very well.

What TensorLogic does is say these are actually the same thing. A logical rule, a Datalog rule for example, is really an Einstein summation over Boolean tensors. A join in logic is a tensor contraction. Once you see that, you can write the equations and the rules in one language, with one construct, the tensor equation. That means a scientist can write down the known physics or the known domain knowledge directly, as rules or equations, and then learn whatever is missing from data, in the same framework, with the same gradient descent machinery we use in deep learning.

That matters a lot for science, because pure deep learning tends to be a black box. It fits the data but it doesn't respect what we already know, and it doesn't give you something you can read and interpret. Pure symbolic approaches, on the other hand, are brittle and don't learn well. In TensorLogic you get both: the learned model is still a set of tensor equations that you can inspect, which is much closer to what a scientific theory actually looks like.

And there's one more piece I'm quite excited about, which is that you can do reasoning in embedding space. You can take a rule and, by controlling a temperature parameter, make it behave as strict deductive logic, with no hallucination, or relax it so it does analogical reasoning, generalizing from similar objects. Science needs both. You want rigor when you're deriving consequences, and you want analogy when you're forming hypotheses. Having a single language that spans that whole spectrum, and is also efficient on GPUs, is why I think it could become something like the lingua franca for scientific modeling, in the way calculus was for physics.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists can express known physics as rules or equations in TensorLogic, but does not state that its tensor equations translate page-written scientific equations almost symbol for symbol.

r002.rationale: It says equations and logical rules can be written in one language using the tensor equation construct.

r003.rationale: It explains that logic rules and tensor operations share a framework where missing information can be learned from data using gradient descent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the reason I think tensor logic would be a good language for science is that science is fundamentally about two things. One is formulating hypotheses, which are typically expressed in some kind of symbolic form, in mathematics, in logic, in the language of the field. And the other is learning from data, fitting those hypotheses to observations, and increasingly these days doing that with neural networks and other machine learning methods. And right now those two halves of science live in different worlds. You have the symbolic world of equations and theories and rules, and you have the numeric world of deep learning and tensors and gradient descent, and the two don't talk to each other very well. A scientist who wants to combine them has to do a lot of awkward engineering.

Tensor logic unifies those two things. The key observation is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are really the same operation. When you write a rule in Datalog, you're doing a join followed by a projection, and that's exactly what you're doing when you contract tensors. So in tensor logic you can write down a theory the way you'd write it in logic, as relations and rules, and at the same time everything is a tensor, so it's differentiable, you can learn it from data, you can run it on a GPU. You get the transparency and compositionality of symbolic reasoning together with the scalability and learnability of neural networks, in one language with essentially one construct.

What that means for science is that a scientist can state their prior knowledge, the laws they already believe, the structure of the domain, directly in the model, and then let the data fill in the parts that are unknown. You don't have to choose between a black box that fits the data but that nobody understands, and a hand-built theory that is interpretable but can't absorb the data. And because the reasoning is sound, when the system tells you something you can trace back why. You can actually have it reason about the hypotheses, not just approximate them. I think that's what you want in a language for science: something where a theory is a program, the program is learnable, and the learning is reliable. That's what tensor logic is trying to be.

r001.rationale: The response connects logical rules with tensor contractions, but does not say TensorLogic equations can closely translate scientific equations written on a page.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic unifies symbolic logic and tensor operations in one language, where theories are written as logical rules and everything is a tensor.

r003.rationale: It says TensorLogic is differentiable and learnable from data, and that scientists can put prior knowledge and domain structure directly into the model for the data to fill in.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that science needs both symbolic reasoning and learning from data. We formulate theories in terms of objects, relations, and rules, but we also have measurements, uncertainty, and parameters that we need to estimate. And those activities are often carried out in quite separate languages and tools.

The idea behind TensorLogic is to bring them into one language. You can express logical structure and tensor computations together, so you have a way to connect a theory with the machinery for learning from observations. You can put in what you already know and learn the parts you don’t know.

Think about biology, for example. You might have knowledge about which entities interact, alongside numerical measurements of those interactions. You want to reason about the structure and fit the quantitative model together. A language that makes that connection natural could be useful across many sciences.

That doesn’t mean the language does the science for you. You still need good hypotheses and good experiments. But it could make the cycle of expressing a hypothesis, deriving predictions, and comparing them with data much more seamless.

r001.rationale: It does not say TensorLogic equations translate scientific equations written on a page nearly symbol for symbol.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic brings logical structure and tensor computations together in one language.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning unknown parts, but does not clearly state that the logic surrounding tensor operations is itself learnable.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because science has these two sides to it. On the one hand, you have theories, which describe the world in terms of entities and relationships and rules. And on the other hand, you have measurements, which are numerical, and you want to fit your theories to those measurements. We have very good languages for each of those things separately, but bringing them together is still surprisingly difficult.

The idea with TensorLogic is that logical rules and tensor operations can be expressed in the same language. So you can express the structure of a theory, but you can also do numerical computation and learn parameters from data. You don't have to make this sharp choice between writing down what you know and learning what you don't know.

And that's a very natural fit for science, because science is a constant back-and-forth between those two things. You propose a theory, derive predictions, compare them with observations, and revise the theory. A language that brings those activities together could make that process much easier to automate—and make the resulting models easier to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says theories and measurements can be brought together, but does not state that TensorLogic equations can translate scientific equations almost symbol for symbol.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says logical rules and tensor operations can be expressed in the same language.

r003.rationale: The response says parameters can be learned from data, but does not state that the logic surrounding tensor operations is itself learnable.
